newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FOCUS - IMF urges Israel economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - IMF urges Israel economic reforms.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Wednesday criticised Israel's expansionary fiscal policy of the past two years and urged medium-term reforms to get the economy back on track.
In an interim report, the IMF recommended measures to control public spending in addition to those proposed by the new government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
It also supported the Bank of Israel's tight monetary policy and its stand on lowering inflation in the medium term.

"The Israeli economy is at a pivotal juncture in the rapid, long-term expansion initiated by the large inflow of immigrants in the early 1990s and sustained by the peace process since then," said the report, released at the end of an annual visit by an IMF delegation.
A final report will be presented in Washington before the end of the year.

"Expansionary fiscal policy during the last two years strained the economy's resources...and did so by boosting consumption rather than investment. As a result, the current account deteriorated, spearheaded by a surge in consumer imports and inflation accelerated," the report said.

The IMF weclomed the new government's stated commitment to fiscal consolidation, disinflation and structural reform. If implemented, prospects for these policies succeeding are good but the risks are "considerable", the IMF said.

Netanyahu's government has sent to the Knesset (parliament) a tight budget for 1997 that would cut 4.9 billion shekels or 3.2 percent of spending, excluding debt servicing. The Knesset has until the end of the year to pass the budget.
Noting that an imbalance in the government's accounts was at the core of current problems, the IMF recommended ways to "hasten and strengthen" the credibility of the budget.

"One possibility would be to accelerate consideration and passage of the budget. Another would be for budget law to explicitly set aside a percentage of planned current expenditures in a special reserve fund that would only be released once the government reported to the Knesset at midyear that the fiscal accounts remained on track".
The IMF said it was essential the government achieve its 1997 deficit target of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product.
The government plans to reduce the deficit target to 1.5 percent by 2001 but the IMF said this was not enough.
"We would urge more ambitious deficit targets both in the medium term -- say balance by 2001 -- and in any one year if favourable economic development permits."
The IMF also urged setting medium-term monetary policy goals, as advocated by the Bank of Israel. Until now the government has set annual inflation targets.
"We would see merit in a framework that aimed to get underlying inflation down to four percent by 2001, with an intermediate target of being below, say, seven percent in 1998," the IMF said.
Inflation this year is expected to exceed the government's 1996 target of 8-10 percent.
The IMF stressed the importance of an independent central bank with effective instruments of monetary control.
In the area of structural reforms, the IMF urged decreasing government intervention in the economy and reducing widespread indexation.
($1 = 3.17 shekels)
